title: Proverbs
subtitle: Many hands make light work
summary: Learn a set of common English proverbs, what each one means, and how speakers use them to comment on a situation.

lesson.heading: What proverbs are for
lesson.text: A **proverb** is a short, fixed saying that offers advice or a warning. Speakers use proverbs to comment on a situation - often at the end of a story someone has told, or in response to an event. They are always quoted word for word.

examples.text: *A:* He's made a fortune from just one little shop! *B:* Well, **take care of the pennies and the pounds will take care of themselves**.
*A:* Everyone arrived at a different time and it was chaos. *B:* **Too many cooks spoil the broth**.

lesson.heading: Advice and warnings
rows: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
Don't depend on something happening, because it may not.
Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Don't invest all your efforts or attention in just one thing.
Never judge a book by its cover.
Don't judge people or things by their outward appearance.
Never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
Never refuse good fortune when it is there in front of you.
Take care of the pennies and the pounds will take care of themselves.
Take care of small sums of money and they will become large sums.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
We'll deal with that problem when it actually happens.

lesson.heading: Key elements: animals and birds
lesson.text: One good way to group proverbs is by a key element they share. Several of the commonest English proverbs involve animals and birds.

examples.text: **When the cat's away, the mice will play.**
examples.note: people take advantage of someone else's absence to behave more freely

examples.text: **You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.**
examples.note: you can try to persuade someone, but you can't force them
one positive sign does not mean that all will be well; a swallow is a bird that returns to Britain in late spring

lesson.heading: Visualising a proverb
lesson.text: As with all vocabulary, picturing the scene in your mind helps you remember the words. Imagine the smoke, the glass house or the crowded kitchen as you learn each of these.

examples.text: **There's no smoke without fire.** / **Where there's smoke, there's fire.**
examples.note: rumours are usually based on some degree of truth

examples.text: **People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.**
examples.note: don't criticise other people's faults if you have the same fault yourself
too many people interfering is a bad way of doing things; broth is a kind of soup
a lot of people helping makes a job easier

lesson.heading: Two proverbs that disagree

left.label: Many hands make light work
left.text: The more helpers there are, the more easily the job gets done.
examples: Thanks for helping with the boxes - many hands make light work.

right.label: Too many cooks spoil the broth
right.text: If too many people are involved in a job, they get in each other's way.
examples: Three people organised the same meeting and it was chaos - too many cooks spoil the broth.

lesson.note: Proverbs are not a system of logic. Speakers simply choose the one that fits the situation.

lesson.heading: Three more proverbs worth knowing
rows: All that glitters is not gold.
Something attractive on the outside may be worthless - close to Never judge a book by its cover.
A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
Take the good thing you already have - close to Never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
Absence makes the heart grow fonder.
You love someone more when you cannot be with them - the opposite idea to When the cat's away, the mice will play.

lesson.text: English speakers often quote only the first half of a proverb - *Well, people who live in glass houses ...* - and leave the listener to supply the rest.

exercises.prompt: Someone says they have just been offered a free two-week holiday, but they are hesitating. Which proverb fits?
options: Never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
One swallow doesn't make a summer.
There's no smoke without fire.
exercises.explanation: Never look a gift-horse in the mouth = never refuse good fortune when it is in front of you.

exercises.prompt: Someone thanks you and your friends for helping to load heavy boxes into a van. Which proverb fits?
options: Many hands make light work.
Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
Never judge a book by its cover.
When the cat's away, the mice will play.
exercises.explanation: Many hands make light work = a job is easier when a lot of people help.

exercises.prompt: Someone says they can't be bothered applying to different universities and will just apply to one. Which proverb fits?
options: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
Many hands make light work.
You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
exercises.explanation: Don't put all your eggs in one basket = don't invest all your effort in just one thing.

exercises.prompt: Three people have made different arrangements for the same meeting, so everyone arrives at a different time and the result is total confusion. Which proverb fits?
options: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Many hands make light work.
All that glitters is not gold.
Take care of the pennies and the pounds will take care of themselves.
exercises.explanation: Too many cooks spoil the broth = too many people interfering is a bad way of doing things.

exercises.prompt: A travelling companion keeps worrying: 'What'll happen if the plane is delayed?', 'What if our luggage gets lost?' Which proverb fits?
options: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
There's no smoke without fire.
One swallow doesn't make a summer.
People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.
exercises.explanation: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it = we'll deal with that problem when it actually happens.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Joel's always criticising people who are selfish, yet he's terribly selfish himself. *B:* Yes, well, people who live in glass houses ___.
exercises.explanation: Don't criticise other people's faults if you have the same fault yourself.

exercises.prompt: *A:* The people in the office have been playing computer games all day since the boss fell ill. *B:* Well, you know what they say: when the cat's away ___.
exercises.explanation: When the cat's away, the mice will play = people take advantage of someone's absence.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I didn't believe those rumours about Nick and Tara, but apparently they are seeing each other. *B:* You know what they say, where there's smoke, ___.
exercises.explanation: Rumours are usually based on some degree of truth.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Amazing, he's made a fortune from just one little shop! *B:* Well, I think it's a case of take care of the pennies and ___.
answers: the pounds will take care of themselves
exercises.explanation: Look after small sums of money and they grow into large ones.

exercises.prompt: Match each proverb with its meaning.

pairs.left: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
pairs.right: Don't depend on something happening - it may not.

pairs.left: Never judge a book by its cover.
pairs.right: Don't judge things by their outward appearance.

pairs.left: One swallow doesn't make a summer.
pairs.right: One good sign does not mean all will be well.

pairs.left: You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
pairs.right: You can persuade someone but you can't force them.
A job is easier when lots of people help.

exercises.prompt: Another common proverb is *All that glitters is not gold*. Which proverb on this page has a similar meaning?
options: Never judge a book by its cover.
Many hands make light work.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
When the cat's away, the mice will play.
exercises.explanation: Both warn against trusting how something looks on the outside.

exercises.prompt: Another common proverb is *A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush*. Which proverb has a similar meaning?
options: Never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
There's no smoke without fire.
Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
exercises.explanation: Both advise you to take advantage of the good fortune you already have.

exercises.statement: *Absence makes the heart grow fonder* and *When the cat's away, the mice will play* mean roughly the same thing.
exercises.explanation: They are opposites: the first says you love someone more when they are away, the second says people take advantage of their absence.

exercises.prompt: Put the proverb in order. (A job is easier when lots of people help.)
exercises.explanation: Many hands make light work - the opposite idea to Too many cooks spoil the broth.

exercises.prompt: Which two proverbs warn against anticipating the future, and which two are about how things look or sound?

items.text: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
Never judge a book by its cover.
